specPoints.text: describe how to carry out a flame test
know the colours formed in flame tests for these cations: Li+ is red; Na+ is yellow; K+ is lilac; Ca2+ is orange-red; Cu2+ is blue-green

primer.text: From Tests for Gases you already know that gases betray themselves with splints and litmus paper. This note moves from gases to solids, where the metal ion paints the Bunsen flame itself in a colour that names it.

lessons.title: How to carry out a flame test
lessons.opening: A flame test identifies which metal cation is present by the colour the sample paints onto a Bunsen flame. The wire loop is cleaned in dilute acid and burned clean in the blue flame first, because any leftover ions would add their own colours and mask the one you need to see. Only then is the loop dipped into the sample and held at the flame's edge.
keyPoints: The flame test identifies positive metal ions by flame colour.
The loop is made of unreactive wire, commonly nichrome or platinum.
The wire is dipped in dilute acid and held in the blue flame until no colour shows.
The sample is picked up on the loop and placed at the edge of the blue flame.
Cleaning in acid first prevents contamination from ions already on the wire.

low.restatement: Clean a wire loop in dilute acid, heat it in the blue flame until it glows with no colour, dip it in the sample, then hold it at the edge of the blue flame and read the colour.
low.analogy: Cleaning the loop first is like wiping a paintbrush clean before dipping it: any old colour left on the bristles would muddy the new one.
low.examPointer: Method marks sit in the order clean, heat clean, dip, test, so write the sequence as separate steps.

medium.restatement: The acid wash dissolves ionic leftovers off the wire, and the flame check proves the loop is clean before anything is sampled. Two or more ions on the wire together would each add their colour, and one colour could mask another, so the test would fail at the very step it is meant to succeed.
medium.analogy: It is the same reason a chef tastes from a clean spoon every time: a spoon that has met one dish already carries its flavour into the next judgement.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the acid cleaning matters, answer in terms of mixed or masked colours, not in terms of hygiene or safety.

check.stem: Why is the wire loop cleaned in dilute acid before use?

options.text: To remove ions that would contaminate the flame colour
options.explanation: Leftover ions would burn with their own colours and spoil the reading.

options.text: To make the wire conduct electricity
options.explanation: No electricity flows in a flame test; conduction is irrelevant.
The acid wash is about cleanliness, not temperature.

options.text: To add sodium colour to the flame
options.explanation: Adding colour is the opposite of the cleaning step's purpose.

check.stem: What is seen when the clean loop is first held in the blue flame?

options.explanation: A clean loop burns without adding any colour of its own.
A lilac flash would mean potassium ions are still on the wire.
A yellow glow would mean sodium contamination, so the loop is not clean.
A clean wire does not extinguish the flame.
Both are unreactive and add no colour of their own.
Copper would colour the flame blue-green itself and ruin the reading.
A sodium coating guarantees a yellow flame regardless of the sample.
Only unreactive wires qualify; random wire risks its own colour.

check.stem: Where in the flame is the sample held?

options.text: At the edge of the blue flame
options.explanation: The method places the loaded loop at the edge of the hot blue flame.
The yellow flame is cooler and adds its own glow; the test needs blue.
The sample must meet the hot gases to give its colour.

options.text: Under the barrel of the burner
options.explanation: That is where the air hole is, not a testing position.

check.stem: What happens if two different ions sit on the wire together?

options.text: Their colours mix and can mask each other
options.explanation: One colour can hide another, which is exactly why cleaning matters.

options.text: The stronger ion destroys the other
options.explanation: Ions do not destroy each other on the wire; they both colour the flame.

options.text: Both colours appear separately in bands
options.explanation: Flames show blended colour, not separated bands.

options.text: Nothing, only one ion can colour a flame
options.explanation: Every ion present contributes, which is the problem being avoided.

lessons.title: The five cation colours
lessons.opening: Five cations and their flame colours make up the table to learn: lithium burns red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper(II) blue-green. The colours only show properly on a hot blue flame, so the Bunsen air hole is opened before testing. Mixing up yellow and orange-red, or lilac and blue-green, costs the mark.
keyPoints: Lithium ions colour the flame red.
Sodium ions colour the flame yellow.
Potassium ions colour the flame lilac.
Calcium ions colour the flame orange-red.
Copper(II) ions colour the flame blue-green.

low.restatement: The colour table is short and fixed: Li+ red, Na+ yellow, K+ lilac, Ca2+ orange-red, Cu2+ blue-green. Heat the sample strongly on a blue flame, then match the colour you see to the table without second-guessing.
low.analogy: The five colours are like five uniforms on a sports field: once the shirts are learned, a single glance tells you which team, which ion, is playing.
low.examPointer: Spell lilac correctly and write orange-red and blue-green as the two-word colours, because vague answers such as reddish lose marks.

medium.restatement: Each cation has a fixed colour because its electrons release a characteristic set of wavelengths when the flame heats them. The pairs most often confused are the two reds, lithium versus calcium's orange-red, and the two cools, potassium's lilac versus copper(II)'s blue-green, so anchoring one member of each pair first makes the table stick.
medium.analogy: Think of the colours as signatures on cheques: lithium signs in plain red while calcium adds orange to its red, and potassium signs in soft lilac while copper(II) adds green to its blue.
medium.examPointer: If a description says brick-red or orange, decide between Li+ and Ca2+ by the orange component; blue-green always points to Cu2+.

check.stem: Which cation gives a lilac flame?

options.explanation: Potassium ions colour the flame lilac.
Sodium gives yellow, not lilac.
Lithium gives red, not lilac.
Calcium gives orange-red, not lilac.

check.stem: Which cation gives an orange-red flame?

options.explanation: Calcium ions colour the flame orange-red.
Copper(II) gives blue-green, not orange-red.
Lithium gives plain red without the orange component.
Potassium gives lilac.

check.stem: Which cation gives a blue-green flame?

options.explanation: Copper(II) ions colour the flame blue-green.
Sodium gives yellow.
Lithium gives red.
Calcium gives orange-red.

check.stem: A sample burns with a red-orange colour. Which ion is present?

options.explanation: Orange-red is calcium's signature colour.
Lithium's red carries no orange component.
Sodium's yellow is clearly distinct from orange-red.
Potassium's lilac is nowhere near orange.

check.stem: Why must the flame be blue and hot?

options.text: The sample needs strong heating for the colour to show
options.explanation: The hot blue flame excites the ions enough to emit their colours.

options.text: Blue flames burn cooler, protecting the sample
options.explanation: The blue flame is the hotter one; the statement inverts the physics.

options.text: The yellow flame adds its own colour
options.explanation: The cooler luminous flame is avoided, but the reason given for the blue flame is the strong heating it supplies.

options.text: Colours only exist in blue light
options.explanation: The colours come from the ions, not from the flame's own hue.

glossary.definition: A test that identifies a metal cation from the colour its sample gives a Bunsen flame.
A positive ion, here the metal ion whose colour identifies it.
An unreactive nickel-chromium alloy used for the flame-test wire loop.
An unreactive metal that can also be used for the flame-test loop.
Leftover ions on the wire that add or mask colours during the test.
